analysis.one_liner: Bans insurance companies and pharmacy benefit managers from owning pharmacies, forcing divestment within three years.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for a company to own both a pharmacy and either a health insurance company or a pharmacy benefit manager — the middlemen who negotiate drug prices and pay pharmacy claims for health plans. Companies caught in both businesses, such as insurers that also run retail, mail-order, and specialty pharmacies, would have three years to sell off the pharmacy side. Enforcers — the FTC, the Justice Department's antitrust division, the HHS Inspector General, and state attorneys general — could sue violators, force divestment, and claw back pharmacy revenue earned during the violation, with recovered money redistributed to help the overcharged community. The FTC would review every divestiture to make sure it doesn't just hand the pharmacy to another dominant player.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent and neighborhood pharmacies that compete against insurer-owned pharmacies, and patients who fill prescriptions — the bill targets the conflict of interest that arises when the company that decides what a pharmacy gets paid also owns its competitors and steers patients to its own stores.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits common ownership of pharmacies and insurance companies or pharmacy benefit managers, with divestment required within three years of enactment [S2].

Lets the FTC, DOJ Antitrust Division, HHS Inspector General, and state attorneys general sue violators, win cease-and-desist orders, force divestment, and disgorge pharmacy revenue earned during the violation [S2].
Directs disgorged revenue to an FTC-administered fund for the health care needs of the harmed community, explicitly including consumers overcharged at vertically integrated pharmacies [S2].

Requires FTC and DOJ review of every divestiture — without the usual size thresholds — to check its effect on competition and the public interest, and lets the FTC write rules to carry out the ban [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The large vertically integrated companies that own insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, and pharmacy businesses would have to divest their pharmacies within three years, forfeit the strategy of steering patients to in-house drug dispensing, and face disgorgement of pharmacy revenue if they violate the ban.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers that own PBMs and pharmacies

drawbacks.text: The ban is written broadly: it covers retail, mail-order, specialty, hospital, and long-term care pharmacies under common ownership with any insurer or PBM, so some integrated systems could face costly and complicated divestitures on a three-year clock, with the divestment deadline extended only during FTC/DOJ merger review [S2].

Defenders of vertical integration argue that one company covering insurance, pharmacy benefit management, and drug dispensing can offer lower prices and one-stop convenience; forcing divestment could disrupt services for some patients and eliminate bundled savings, a cost the bill does not weigh directly [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real conflict of interest — middlemen that both negotiate drug prices and own the pharmacies those prices apply to — and backs it with real enforcement teeth, including revenue clawbacks and community compensation. The trade-off is disruption: broad divestment on a fixed timeline could create transition costs and might unwind some integration that, at least in some cases, delivered convenience or savings. On balance the anti-monopoly protections address a documented driver of high drug costs, but the bill never advanced far enough to be tested or refined.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on December 12, 2024, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill for herself and Sen. Josh Hawley on December 12, 2024 [S1].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S4].
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Vertically integrated insurers and pharmacy benefit managers keep their pharmacy businesses, and independent pharmacies keep competing against owner-controlled networks. Patients see no change in the pharmacy market. Congress had already passed a narrower version of this idea — the Pharmacy Benefit Manager Reform Act's ban on PBM-insurer-pharmacy consolidation was stripped from a December 2024 spending package — so the concentrated interests kept the integrated model intact through the end of the session.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar common ownership of pharmacies and insurers/PBMs and referred it to Judiciary [S1] [S2].

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat (Warren) and a Republican (Hawley) co-sponsored the bill, but no committee action or vote ever followed, so no partisan divide appears in the record.

industries.industry: Vertically integrated insurers that also own PBMs and pharmacies (retail, mail-order, specialty)
industries.note: The bill forces these conglomerates to sell off their pharmacy operations within three years and exposes them to disgorgement of pharmacy revenue if they violate the ban, dismantling the model of steering insured patients to company-owned drug dispensing. Their interest in keeping the integrated model runs against the bill's goal of protecting pharmacy competition and patient pricing.

PBMs are barred from common ownership with pharmacies, limiting their ability to own the dispensing businesses they steer patients toward, though their core negotiating and claims-administration business remains legal. The bill's definition of 'pharmacy benefit manager' is broad, reaching third-party administrators regardless of what they call themselves [S2].

These pharmacies compete directly against insurer-owned drugstores and mail-order operations; removing the owner's ability to funnel patients to its own pharmacies would ease that pressure. They also gain access to the FTC-run compensation fund for overcharged communities if violations are proven.
